transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: A new study has found that spending time in nature—even just two hours a week—can significantly improve both physical and mental health, according to researchers at the University of Exeter. The study surveyed over 20,000 people and found that those who spent at least two hours a week in natural environments like parks, forests, or beaches reported significantly better health and higher psychological well-being than those who spent less time in nature. The benefits were seen across all age groups, both men and women, and people with different income levels and health statuses. Researchers say that spending time in nature reduces stress, lowers blood pressure, boosts the immune system, and improves mood. They note that you don't have to go hiking in the wilderness to get the benefits—even a walk in a local park can make a difference. The study adds to growing evidence that access to nature is important for human health and well-being.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What did the University of Exeter study find about spending time in nature?
2. Why might spending time in nature be good for health according to researchers?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: The city of Seattle has become the latest major US city to ban single-use plastic straws and utensils in restaurants and food service businesses, as part of efforts to reduce plastic pollution and protect the environment. The ban applies to all restaurants, cafes, food trucks, and other food service businesses, which can no longer provide plastic straws, forks, knives, and spoons unless a customer specifically asks for them. Instead, businesses are encouraged to use paper, compostable, or reusable alternatives. The city says that single-use plastics are a major source of pollution, especially in oceans and waterways, where they harm wildlife and take hundreds of years to break down. Supporters of the ban say it's an important step toward reducing plastic waste and protecting the environment. Critics, however, argue that the ban is inconvenient and that the alternatives are more expensive and less effective.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Researchers at Stanford University have developed a new type of flexible, wearable battery that can be stretched, bent, and even washed without losing its ability to hold a charge, according to a new study. Unlike traditional batteries, which are rigid and can break if bent or dropped, this new battery is made of flexible, stretchable materials that can conform to the body. The battery uses a special type of polymer that's both flexible and conductive, and it can be stretched to twice its original size without damaging it. Researchers say that this type of flexible battery could be used in wearable electronics like smart watches, fitness trackers, and even medical devices that are worn on the body. The technology is still in the early stages of development, but researchers are optimistic that it could lead to a new generation of wearable electronics that are more comfortable and durable.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Jessica): Hey Ryan, how's the new job going? You've been there what, three months now?
Man (Ryan): Ugh, honestly? Not great. I mean, it's okay, but I'm not sure it's what I want to do long-term.
Woman: Oh no, that's too bad. What's wrong? I thought you were excited about the marketing position.

Man: I was excited at first. The pay is good, the benefits are great, and the people are nice. But the work itself... I don't know, it's just not very fulfilling. I feel like I'm just pushing papers around and going to meetings all day.
Woman: Hmm, I know what you mean. I've felt that way at jobs before too. What specifically don't you like about it?

Man: Well, I thought marketing would be more creative, but it's actually a lot of data analysis and reporting. And I feel like the work doesn't really matter—like we're just trying to sell people stuff they don't need. I want to do something that makes a real difference, you know?
Woman: Yeah, I get that. It's important to feel like your work has meaning. Have you talked to your boss about maybe taking on different projects?

Man: I've thought about it, but I don't think there's really much room to move around. The company is pretty big and everyone has their specific role. I don't want to be stuck doing this for the next five years.
Woman: So what are you thinking? Are you going to look for another job?
Man: I'm not sure. I don't want to quit without having something else lined up, especially since the pay is good. But I'm starting to think maybe marketing isn't the right field for me.
Woman: Hmm, that's a big decision. What would you do instead? Do you have any ideas?

Man: I've been thinking about maybe going back to school to get a master's degree in public health or environmental policy. I've always been interested in those areas, and I feel like that kind of work would be more meaningful.
Woman: That sounds like a good fit for you. You've always cared about social and environmental issues. But going back to school is a big commitment—time, money...
Man: Yeah, I know. That's why I'm not sure. It would be a lot of work, and I'd probably have to take out loans. And I'm not even sure what I'd do with the degree after.

Woman: Well, maybe you don't have to make a huge decision right away. Could you start by taking a class or two at a community college to see if you like it? Or volunteer somewhere in that field to get some experience?
Man: That's a good idea. I could test the waters without committing to a whole degree program.

Woman: Yeah, exactly. And you could also look for jobs that combine marketing with something you care about—like marketing for a non-profit or an environmental organization. That way you could use your existing skills but work on something more meaningful.
Man: Oh, that's a great point! I hadn't thought about that. I could look for marketing jobs at non-profits or social enterprises. That might be a good middle ground.
Woman: Definitely. There are lots of organizations that need good marketers but are doing work that matters. You don't have to completely change fields to find more meaningful work.

Man: Yeah, you're right. That's probably a better first step than quitting and going back to school right away. I can start looking for other marketing jobs at organizations I care about, and if that doesn't work out, then I can think about going back to school.
Woman: That sounds like a solid plan. And hey, it's okay that you don't have it all figured out. Most people change careers a few times these days.
Man: Yeah, I guess so. Thanks for listening, Jessica. It helps to talk it through.
Woman: No problem! Let me know if you want help with your resume or anything. I'm happy to help.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. What is Ryan considering doing instead?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Liam): Hey Emma, I need your help. I'm working on a history paper about the Industrial Revolution, and I'm feeling really overwhelmed. There's so much information and I don't know where to start.
Woman (Emma): Oh, the Industrial Revolution is a huge topic—no wonder you're overwhelmed. What's the paper about exactly? Do you have a specific thesis or question?
Man: Not really. The assignment just says to write about the environmental impact of the Industrial Revolution. But that's still really broad. I don't know how to narrow it down.

Woman: Yeah, that's a common problem. The key is to find a specific angle instead of trying to cover everything. Let's think... environmental impact. What aspects interest you most? Air pollution? Water pollution? Deforestation?
Man: Hmm, I'm not sure. Maybe air pollution? I've read a little bit about how bad the smog was in cities like London during the Industrial Revolution.
Woman: That's a great topic! London's "pea soup" fog is really interesting. You could write about how coal burning caused terrible air pollution, and how that affected people's health and daily life.
Man: Yeah, that does sound interesting. But I'm worried there won't be enough information, or that it's too narrow.

Woman: Are you kidding? There's tons of information about that. You could talk about the Great Smog of 1952, even though that's after the main Industrial Revolution period, it's a continuation of the same problem. And you could talk about how the government eventually responded with clean air laws.
Man: That sounds good. But how do I structure the paper? I always struggle with organization.

Woman: Well, a typical history paper has an introduction with your thesis statement, then several body paragraphs that support your thesis, and then a conclusion. For your topic, your thesis could be something like: "The Industrial Revolution's reliance on coal caused severe air pollution in British cities, leading to widespread health problems and eventually prompting government action."
Man: That's a good thesis. Then what would the body paragraphs be about?

Woman: Let's see... First, you could set the context—how the Industrial Revolution led to urbanization and increased coal use. Then you could talk about the air pollution itself—what it was like, how bad it got. Then you could talk about the health effects—respiratory diseases, child mortality, things like that. And then you could talk about the response—how people reacted, what the government did, the Clean Air Acts.
Man: That makes sense. What about sources? Where should I look for information?

Woman: Start with the library catalog and the academic databases. JSTOR is great for history papers. And make sure you're using scholarly sources—books and journal articles, not just random websites. Your professor will want to see that you've done real research.
Man: Yeah, I know. But I'm not very good at finding sources. I always end up with either too many or too few.

Woman: That's normal. Start with a few key search terms: "Industrial Revolution air pollution," "London smog," "Great Smog 1952," "Clean Air Act." And then look at the bibliographies of the books and articles you find—they'll lead you to more sources.
Man: That's a good tip. What about citations? I always get confused about how to format them correctly.

Woman: Are you using Chicago style? That's standard for history papers. Just make sure you're consistent—use the same format for all your citations. And there are lots of good guides online, or you can use citation software like Zotero to help.
Man: Thanks, Emma. You're really good at this. How do you know so much about writing history papers?
Woman: Ha, I've written enough of them! I was a history major, remember? And I worked as a writing tutor for a while.
Man: Oh right, I forgot. Would you maybe be willing to look at my paper once I have a draft? I'd really appreciate your feedback.
Woman: Sure, no problem. Just send it to me when you're ready. But give me a few days to look it over, okay?
Man: Absolutely. Thank you so much, Emma. I feel a lot less overwhelmed now.
Woman: No problem! Happy to help. And remember—just start writing. You can always revise later. The hardest part is getting the first draft down.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous and impressive structures in the world, but there are also many myths and misconceptions about it. While it's often called the "Great Wall," it's actually not a single, continuous wall—it's a series of walls, fortifications, and natural barriers built over many centuries by different Chinese dynasties.

One of the most common myths about the Great Wall is that it's visible from space with the naked eye. This is a widely repeated claim, but it's simply not true. Astronauts have confirmed that you can't see the Great Wall from the moon, and it's very difficult to see even from low Earth orbit without binoculars or a camera. The wall is only about 6 to 7 meters wide, which is too narrow to be visible from that distance. It's like trying to see a single hair from a kilometer away.

Another myth is that the Great Wall was built all at once by a single emperor. In reality, the wall was built and rebuilt over a period of more than 2,000 years, starting as early as the 7th century BC. Different dynasties built different sections, and many of the walls were not connected. The most famous sections that people visit today were mostly built during the Ming Dynasty, from the 14th to the 17th centuries.

People also often think that the Great Wall successfully kept invaders out of China. But in reality, the wall was only partially effective. While it did help defend against smaller raids, it wasn't able to stop major invasions. The Mongols, the Manchus, and other groups were able to get past the wall many times, either by finding weak points, bribing guards, or simply going around the ends of the wall. The wall was more of a psychological barrier and a symbol of Chinese power than an impenetrable military defense.

Despite these myths, the Great Wall is still an incredible feat of engineering and a testament to the hard work and ingenuity of the people who built it. It stretches for thousands of kilometers across mountains, deserts, and plains, and it's rightfully considered one of the wonders of the world. It's just important to separate fact from fiction when we talk about it.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Color psychology is the study of how colors affect our emotions, behavior, and perceptions. While the idea that colors can influence our mood and behavior might sound like pseudoscience to some, there's actually real scientific research showing that colors can have measurable effects on how we think, feel, and act.

One of the most well-known effects of color is its impact on mood. Warm colors like red, orange, and yellow tend to be stimulating and energizing. Red is often associated with passion, excitement, and even danger—it can increase heart rate and blood pressure. Yellow is associated with happiness, optimism, and creativity. Orange is somewhere in between, combining the energy of red with the cheerfulness of yellow.

Cool colors like blue, green, and purple, on the other hand, tend to be calming and relaxing. Blue is often associated with trust, stability, and peace—it's one of the most popular colors for corporate logos because it conveys reliability. Green is associated with nature, growth, and health—it's often used in healthcare and environmental branding. Purple is associated with luxury, creativity, and spirituality.

But the effects of color are more complex than just "warm colors are exciting, cool colors are calming." Different shades and tones can have very different effects. A bright, saturated blue can be energizing, while a soft, muted blue can be calming. And context matters too—the same color can mean different things in different situations and cultures.

Culture is actually a very important factor in how we perceive color. While some color associations seem to be universal, others vary widely from culture to culture. For example, in Western cultures, white is associated with purity and weddings, but in many Eastern cultures, white is associated with death and mourning. Red is considered lucky and celebratory in China, but in many Western countries it's associated with danger and warning.

Color also affects our behavior in practical ways. Studies have shown that people are more likely to buy products in certain colors, that students perform differently in classrooms painted different colors, and that even sports teams wearing certain colors win more often. For example, some studies have found that teams wearing red uniforms win more often, possibly because red is associated with dominance and aggression.

Of course, color psychology isn't an exact science. The effects of color are often subtle, and they vary from person to person based on personal experience, culture, and individual preferences. But understanding how colors can influence us can be useful in many areas, from design and marketing to education and healthcare.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Urban agriculture—the practice of growing food in cities—has been growing in popularity around the world as people look for ways to eat healthier, reduce their environmental impact, and build stronger communities. From small backyard gardens to large community farms to rooftop gardens on office buildings, urban agriculture takes many forms and offers many benefits.

One of the most obvious benefits of urban agriculture is that it provides fresh, healthy food to city residents. In many cities, especially in low-income neighborhoods, it can be hard to find fresh fruits and vegetables—these areas are often called "food deserts." Community gardens and urban farms can help address this problem by growing fresh produce locally and making it available to people who live nearby.

Urban agriculture also has environmental benefits. Growing food locally reduces the distance food has to travel from farm to table, which cuts down on transportation emissions and packaging waste. Urban gardens can also help reduce the "heat island" effect in cities, where buildings and pavement absorb heat and make cities hotter than surrounding rural areas. Plants and trees provide shade and cool the air through transpiration. And urban gardens can help manage stormwater by absorbing rainwater that would otherwise run off into streets and sewers.

Another important benefit of urban agriculture is its social impact. Community gardens bring people together from different backgrounds and neighborhoods, creating opportunities for social connection and community building. They give people a chance to work together, share knowledge and skills, and take pride in their neighborhood. For children, gardens are a great way to learn about where food comes from and to develop healthy eating habits.

Urban agriculture can also have economic benefits. It can create jobs in farming, distribution, and food processing. It can help low-income families save money on groceries by growing their own food. And it can increase property values and revitalize blighted areas by turning empty lots into green spaces.

Of course, urban agriculture also faces challenges. Space is limited in cities, and good land can be hard to find and expensive. Soil quality can be poor, and there can be concerns about contamination from previous land use. Water access can also be a problem. And urban farmers often have to deal with pests, weather, and other challenges that all farmers face.

But despite these challenges, urban agriculture continues to grow and evolve. New technologies like hydroponics, vertical farming, and rooftop greenhouses are making it possible to grow more food in less space. And as more people recognize the benefits of growing food locally, urban agriculture is likely to become an increasingly important part of city life.
